10.1002_adma.75533: Lithium (Li) metal has emerged as the premier anode candidate in next-generation high-energy-density batteries due to its ultrahigh theoretical capacity and ultralow electrochemical potential. However, critical technical barriers persist in Li metal anode implementation, such as uncontrolled Li dendrite growth and persistent interfacial side reactions. Acting as the mediating agent between cathodes and anodes, electrolytes critically determine battery overall performance. Taking solvent-salt-additive components as the entry point, adopting liquid-phase electrolyte engineering strategies to optimize electrolyte composition and regulate solvation structure can not only address the inherent issues of Li metal anodes, but also endow Li metal batteries with desired performances, including high safety, high-voltage tolerance, fast-charging capability, and wide-temperature operation. In this review, the design principles of reliable liquid-phase electrolytes for Li metal batteries are discussed in detail. The essential liquid-phase electrolyte engineering strategies, including designing new-type salt/solvent molecular architectures, restructuring salt-solvent combination systems, incorporating electrolyte additives with various functions, utilizing (localized) high-concentration electrolytes, and developing brand-new electrolyte formulations for adapting to different temperature ranges, are comprehensively summarized. Moreover, emerging design strategies, future design considerations, and remaining challenges in electrolyte engineering are highlighted, with the aim of pointing out potential opportunities to propel the practical development of Li metal batteries.
10.1016_j.seppur.2026.140544: Thin-layer coatings from blends of cellulose nanofibers (CNF) and 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine 1-oxyl (TEMPO)-oxidized CNFs (TCNFs) offer a scalable route to ultrafiltration membranes but tuning the membrane performance remains challenging due to poorly understood structure-property-performance relationships. Nanocellulose swelling and non-trivial wet-state pore structure complicate balancing the trade-off between membrane rejection and permeance, and the coating stability under harsh washing remains uncharted. We used statistical experimental design to study how coating composition, thickness and pre-swelling affect the specific permeance and rejection of nanocellulose-coated polyethersulfone membranes. We confirmed that thinner coatings increase specific permeance and discovered that pre-swelling may decrease size exclusion, highlighting how nanocellulose-water interactions shape the membranes' performance. Furthermore, we applied a wet-state pore size analysis for nanocellulose-coated membranes with liquid-liquid displacement porometry to relate the membranes' structure with their properties and performance. The pore size of the nanoscale coatings appeared similar to the nanocellulose width. Coating homogeneity and performance were enhanced from laboratory by roll-to-roll pilot manufacturing, resulting in molecular weight cut-offs <10 kDa, pure water permeances from ~100 to >300 L m −2 h −1 MPa −1 and pore sizes of ~5 nm. Thinner coatings (~100 nm) yielded higher pure water permeance and size-based rejections, while thicker coatings (≥500 nm) showcased lower size-based rejections, but enhanced electrostatic rejection of 0.01 mM Na 2 SO 4 via elevated surface charge. The rejections were comparable with commercial ultrafiltration membranes. Finally, we validated that an established anchoring and acid-induced crosslinking strategy resulted in coatings that tolerated 2 MPa pressure and short-term chemical washing at pH 2 and pH 12.
10.1021_jacs.5c20477: The pursuit of sustainable electrification calls for advanced batteries that deliver high energy density, intrinsic safety, and a sustainable material supply. Conversion-type chemistries enable multielectron transfer and high energy density, yet their reversibility is fundamentally limited by phase segregation of conversion products, driven by agglomeration-induced deactivation and the dissolution of soluble intermediates. In this work, we overcome this central bottleneck in the natural pyrite (FeS 2 ) by introducing a partitioned ionic-cluster electrolyte. This tailored chemical environment suppresses polysulfide dissolution, resulting in a homogeneous nanoscale phase distribution during cycling. Such suppression of phase segregation enables the pyrite cathode to deliver a specific energy of ∼1300 Wh kg –1 over 500 cycles and to retain 72.4% of its capacity after 10,000 cycles at 10C. Moreover, scalable pouch cells demonstrate a competitive energy density of 511 Wh kg –1 and intrinsic safety after nail penetration. This study highlights that electrolyte-enabled phase-segregation suppression is crucial for unlocking the practical potential of earth-abundant conversion-type electrodes.
